newsitem.title: USA: Wallace says Wyser-Pratte proposals defeated.
newsitem.headline: Wallace says Wyser-Pratte proposals defeated.

text.p: Wallace Computer Services Inc said Wednesday that two shareholder proposals aimed at changing the company's takeover defense were defeated at the annual meeting.

Based on preliminary results, a proposal by Wyser-Pratt & Co to require Wallace to opt out of Section 203 of Delaware General Corporation law was defeated, having received 25 percent of the vote, a Wallace spokesman said.
A second proposal, known as the tender offer proposal, was also defeated, receiving about 36 percent of the vote, he added.
Section 203 of the law provides anti-takeover, or poison pill, defenses for Wallace, which last year fended off an unsolicited bid from Moore Corp Ltd.

Under Section 203, any party acquiring 15 percent or more of the company's outstanding shares may engage in a business combination with the company for three years. That provision is subject to certain exceptions.
Wyser-Pratte's tender offer proposal was aimed at forcing Wallace to drop all defenses to a hostile offer after 90 days unless specifically approved by special shareholder vote.

Wallace also said that shareholders approved its three nominees as directors, who received more than 80 percent of the votes. The nominees are Bob Cronin, Wallace president and chief executive officer; Richard Doyle, who has been a director since 1971, and Neele Stearns Jr., who was a director from 1990 until 1995.
A slate of Wyser-Pratte nominees was defeated.
"We are elated that shareholders confirmed our belief that there is no place for takeover speculators on Wallace's board," Ted Dimitrious, chairman, said in a statement.
On November 5, Wyser-Pratte had predicted that its proposals to limit takeover defenses for the business forms maker would be approved.

Eric Longmeire, senior managing director of Wyser-Pratte, said November 5 that most major shareholders were in favor of a proposal requiring Wallace to drop its poison pill defense in 90 days if it receives an all-cash offer of a 25 percent premium over the stock's average price over the past 30 days before the offer is submitted.
A Wallace spokesman said the annual meeting will be reconvened on November 20 when it will certify the shareholder vote.
